title: Australia’s economic pessimism is about more than numbers
gist: The 2026 Lowy Poll shows a record 60% of Australians pessimistic about the next five years of economic performance — worse than during Covid or the GFC — driven not by recession but by falling real wages since 2021, negative productivity since 2019, and a belief that the global conditions underpinning four decades of prosperity are eroding, with almost 75% now backing a 90-day oil stockpile costing A$20 billion.

themes.theme: Record pessimism in the Lowy Poll

insights.claim: The 2026 Lowy Poll found a record 60% of Australians pessimistic about Australia's economic performance over the next five years, higher than at any prior point in the poll's history including the Covid-19 pandemic and the global financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Sentiment worse than during two actual crises, absent recession, signals structural rather than cyclical demand weakness in Australian consumption.
insights.locator: So it is not surprising that the 2026 Lowy Poll

insights.claim: For the first time in the Lowy Poll's history, a majority of Australians feel unsafe in the world today, with a global economic downturn ranked the second-highest perceived threat to Australia behind cyberattacks from other countries.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Threat perception is now economic and cyber rather than military — supports political demand for resilience spending over conventional defence.
insights.locator: Another first for the Lowy Poll

insights.claim: Most Australians do not trust either China or the United States to act responsibly in the world, and trust in their leaders is currently even lower than trust in the countries themselves.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Erosion of trust in both superpowers gives Australian governments political licence for hedging and supply-chain diversification policies.
insights.locator: The Lowy Poll shows most Australians do not trust

insights.claim: Australian real wages have been falling since 2021 and are expected to keep falling through 2026 as the energy shock from the Iran war ripples through the global economy.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: A fifth consecutive year of real wage decline caps discretionary consumption and supports defensive positioning in Australian consumer exposure.
insights.locator: Australian's purchasing power is not what it used to be

insights.claim: Australian labour productivity has gone backwards since 2019, which the author reads as a sign that real wages are unlikely to recover soon, leaving Australia one of the worst-performing countries in the OECD on these metrics.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Negative productivity is the mechanism blocking wage recovery — no cyclical rebound thesis works without a productivity inflection.
insights.locator: Labour productivity has also gone backwards since 2019

insights.claim: A A$100,000 salary in Australia, once a guarantee of a comfortable life, no longer necessarily provides one.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Cost-of-living erosion has moved up the income distribution, widening the affected consumer cohort beyond low-income households.
insights.locator: What this means in practice for the everyday worker

insights.claim: Economic pessimism is widespread across the wealthy developed world and has been for some time, with the United Kingdom similarly pessimistic, more than half of Japanese households reporting worsened circumstances in December 2025, almost half of EU respondents holding negative views and expecting further deterioration, and Americans negative since June 2021 — meaning Australia is merely catching up.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Sentiment weakness is a synchronized developed-market phenomenon, not an Australia-specific policy failure — read it as a global demand signal.
insights.quote: A strong sense of economic pessimism is widespread in the wealthy, developed world, and has been for some time; Australia is merely catching up.
insights.locator: Australians are not alone in feeling this way

insights.claim: The number of Americans rating current economic conditions as poor jumped since the start of the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Direct evidence the Iran war energy shock is transmitting into US household sentiment — a channel into consumer spending data.
insights.locator: Americans have been negative about the economy

insights.claim: Australia's four decades of economic success rested on five external conditions — a growing global economy, expanding international trade, rising incomes in Asia, security from major power conflict, and relatively decent governance by global standards — and growing numbers of Australians now believe these conditions will not last.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Names the five variables an Australia bull case actually depends on, all of which are currently deteriorating.
insights.locator: Australia's economic success was underpinned by a growing global economy

insights.claim: The global political and economic order is fragmenting on multiple concrete fronts: US and Chinese belligerence, resurgent US protectionism reinforced by European tariff discussion to meet a China Shock 2.0, global growth slowing again under repeated shocks, the Strait of Hormuz remaining closed, and continued Chinese economic coercion of other countries even though Australia is no longer a target.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: A closed Strait of Hormuz plus European tariffs against Chinese goods are the two hard, tradable facts in the fragmentation thesis.
insights.locator: The global political and economic order is becoming more fragmented

insights.claim: Australians' economic pessimism correlates with growing insecurity because they have been told for decades that prosperity is tied to a rules-based international order, unimpeded sea routes, global growth particularly in Asia, and free trade — all of which are now visibly shifting.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Explains why sentiment is worse than the domestic data alone implies — households are pricing geopolitical regime change, not just wages.
insights.locator: Australians have heard for decades that the country's prosperity

insights.claim: Fuel stockpiling in China — and to a lesser extent South Korea and Japan — was vindicated by the Iran war's energy shock, with Beijing in particular adequately shielding households and the broader economy.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Demonstrated payoff from strategic reserves will drive a wave of state-funded stockpiling demand across importing economies.
insights.locator: Fuel stockpiling in China (and to a lesser extent South Korea and Japan)

insights.claim: Almost 75% of Australians now support building an oil stockpile in line with the International Energy Agency's recommendation of 90 days of emergency fuel use, even at a cost of A$20 billion to taxpayers.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Near-supermajority support at a named A$20 billion price point makes a large Australian strategic petroleum reserve a live procurement opportunity in storage, logistics and crude purchasing.
insights.locator: According to the Lowy Poll, almost 75% of Australians

insights.claim: The European Union has proposed forcing companies to use at least three suppliers for critical components, two of which must be in different geographic locations, as a means of diversifying global value chains and reducing supply chain chokepoints.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: A mandated multi-sourcing rule would force structural reallocation of component purchasing away from single-source Asian suppliers — margin cost for buyers, volume win for second-source vendors.
insights.locator: The European Union's proposed policy that would force companies

insights.claim: Governments need heterodox approaches that reduce dependency risk and promote resilience while preserving the benefits of economic integration, and should start by becoming better at protecting populations from foreseeable shocks — including stockpiling essential inputs beyond fuel.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Signals the direction of Australian industrial policy: state-funded inventory and diversification mandates rather than tariffs.
insights.quote: People want stability and see value in policies that build economic resilience and security.
insights.locator: Governments can start by becoming better at protecting

insights.claim: It is hyperbole to say Australia's prosperity is over, but not hyperbole to say people are more worried than ever that it could disappear.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: The author's calibrated bottom line — a sentiment and political-risk story, not yet a fundamentals collapse.
insights.quote: It is hyperbole to say Australia’s prosperity is over. It is not hyperbole to say that people are more worried than ever that it could disappear.
insights.locator: As the global foundations of Australia's growth erode
